packing: Each embedding is a unit-norm float32 vector of dim values. For every vector the scale is max(abs(v)) / 127; q = round(v / scale) as int8 in [-127, 127]. The q of all vectors are concatenated in order, row-major, and base64 encoded. Decode vector i as v[j] = scale[i] * int8(q[i * dim + j]), j from 0 to dim - 1. Cosine similarity is the dot product after re-normalising the decoded vector.

passages.head: Purpose
passages.text: Organisations keep codified memories, such as taxonomies and classified records, that are maintained for present retrieval yet read as dated histories. This paper asks what maintenance does to measures taken from such a memory, using the patent classification from which knowledge recombination research measures novelty.

passages.head: Design/methodology/approach
passages.text: For 833,267 US patent applications, the association between recombinant novelty and grant is estimated from three dated states of each application’s own classification record, holding documents, outcome and counting rule fixed. Falsification tests were frozen in a pre-analysis plan after exploratory work on the same data.

passages.head: Findings
passages.text: Applications with five or more new code pairs are 3.53 percentage points more likely to be granted than those with none when read from today’s record, and not distinguishably different when read from the record as published. Read at disposition, the gap is 16.77 points: granted records are classified again at the grant, refused ones are not, and later maintenance removes most of that difference. Information provably created after the decision is related to it only within a preregistered equivalence region.

passages.head: Practical implications
passages.text: Users of maintained repositories should state which version a measure is read from and check whether entries are completed on the outcome’s schedule.

passages.head: Originality
passages.text: A codified memory can carry the outcome it is used to explain through when entries are written, not through hindsight revision; the study offers a two-date audit for any versioned knowledge repository.

passages.head: Introduction
passages.text: Organisations keep much of what they know in codified memories maintained for present use: taxonomies that index documents, classifications that route cases, tags that organise knowledge bases. Maintenance keeps such a memory useful, but it also means that an entry read today is not the entry that existed when the events it describes took place. Researchers and managers who read these memories as histories, secondary knowledge miners in Markus’s (2001) terms, therefore measure the state of the memory on the day they read it as well as the past it records.

passages.head: Introduction
passages.text: Organisational memory research has long described memory as information retained from an organisation’s history and retrieved for present decisions (Walsh and Ungson, 1991), a storage view that remains influential beside interpretive accounts (Foroughi et al., 2020). It names maintenance among memory’s functions (Stein and Zwass, 1995) and has called for work on how knowledge becomes embedded in memory over time (Casey and Olivera, 2011). What maintenance does to the measures secondary users take from a codified memory has not, to our knowledge, been tested.

passages.head: Introduction
passages.text: Knowledge recombination research offers a demanding case, and one with many users in this journal (Ju et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2026; Schillaci et al., 2022). It reads patent classification codes as the components an invention joins (Fleming, 2001) and counts as new any pair of codes absent from earlier documents (Strumsky and Lobo, 2015; Verhoeven et al., 2016). The classification it reads is maintained for search: categories are created, merged and retired, documents are moved to the revised scheme, and a granted application is classified again when it is issued (Lafond and Kim, 2019; Persoon, 2026). Unlike most organisational memories, it publishes dated states of each document’s record and the date on which every category came into existence, so when information entered the record can be shown rather than assumed.

passages.head: Introduction
passages.text: The paper asks whether the date at which a maintained codified record is read changes what a measure taken from it says about the outcome it is used to explain, and at which point in the record’s writing the outcome enters. For 833,267 US first filings, applications that continue no earlier one, the same novelty measure is built from three states of each application’s record: as published, at disposition and today (Figure 1). Read today, applications with five or more new code pairs are 3.53 percentage points more likely to be granted than those with none; read as published, the difference is small and not distinguishable from zero. Read at disposition, it is 16.77 points, because a granted application is classified again at its grant and a refused one is not. Later maintenance, which reaches refused records too, removes most of that difference. A falsification test frozen before estimation asked whether information created after the decision is related to it; the association lies inside the preregistered region of practical equivalence.

passages.head: Introduction
passages.text: The paper makes three contributions. For organisational memory and codification, it shows that a maintained memory can carry the outcome it is used to explain through the schedule on which entries are written, without hindsight revision, and that maintenance reaching every entry dilutes rather than creates that dependence. For knowledge measurement, it offers a design any user of a versioned knowledge artefact can apply: one record read at its own dates against a permutation benchmark. For practice, it gives dating rules for those who keep or mine taxonomies, knowledge bases and case records. Nothing is identified causally, and neither state of the record is treated as correct. Section 2 develops the argument, sections 3 and 4 the setting and design, sections 5 to 7 the results, and sections 8 and 9 the implications and limits.

passages.head: Memory as store and as maintained record
passages.text: Walsh and Ungson (1991) located organisational memory in individuals and beyond them, in culture, transformation procedures, structures and the workplace, and described it through acquisition, retention and retrieval. Read strictly as storage, an entry changes only by addition or loss, so a record read today shows what was known at the date it describes. Interpretive accounts hold instead that the past is reached through interpretations of traces such as records and artefacts, which change with present conditions (Foroughi et al., 2020), and Bowker (2005) treats scientific records as resources for the present rather than containers of the past. A functional reading sits between the two: memory systems acquire, retain, maintain, search and retrieve (Stein and Zwass, 1995), and a maintained entry is kept fit for present use. Blagoev et al. (2018) find both sides in one artefact, a museum catalogue that is at once a stored record and a practice of remembering. No study we found tests the readings’ predictions quantitatively on dated states of one codified record against an outcome.

passages.head: Secondary users and the dated-record assumption
passages.text: Secondary knowledge miners extract knowledge from records that others assembled for other purposes (Markus, 2001), and those who take part in constructing a set of codes interpret and use them more similarly than those who do not (Hall, 2006). Validity attaches to the inference rather than to the indicator (Cronbach and Meehl, 1955), validation in one context does not imply validity in another (Adcock and Collier, 2001), and how a construct is operationalised is a largely ignored source of researcher degrees of freedom (Flake and Fried, 2020). Recombination studies read classification codes as a dated record of the invention and, where they address revision, treat the current codes as authoritative (Arts and Veugelers, 2015; Verhoeven et al., 2016), sometimes while disclosing that later categories have been applied to earlier documents (Kim et al., 2026, p. 64). Arts and Veugelers (2015, p. 1227) state the risk against their own design: classification updates create new subclasses and combinations after filing, and such reclassification is likely related to the success of the inventions concerned, although their checks found no evidence of bias (p. 1240).

passages.head: Codification decides what the memory can hold
passages.text: Cowan et al. (2000) treat the boundary between codified and tacit knowledge as set by incentives, so what reaches a record is what somebody had reason to write down. Zollo and Winter (2002) count codification among deliberate learning mechanisms in which organisations invest unevenly. A record therefore holds what was articulated and not the tacit knowledge used beside it (Smith, 2001; Nonaka, 1994), and assigning a case to a category is situated judgement within collectively interpreted rules (Tsoukas and Vladimirou, 2001), with categories that make some features visible and leave others unrepresented (Bowker and Star, 1999, p. 5; Star and Bowker, 2007). The incentive to complete a record can also arrive with a decision. A patent office reviews an application’s classification when it is passed to issue (USPTO, 2024, section 905.03(b)); a refused application never receives that pass.

passages.head: Kept up to date, not kept still
passages.text: Classification systems are a clear case of codified memory that an organisation deliberately maintains. Bowker and Star (1999) describe them as infrastructure: built on an installed base, changed in modular increments and invisible in use until they break down. The past can be reached only through classification systems, and the categories available now are not those available then (p. 41). Patent classifications have been read in this way, with conclusions about green technology that depend on the classification vintage used (Barbieri et al., 2025). For the office that keeps one, a patent classification is the index of its own codified memory, designed and updated for prior-art search, and its reclassification follows the recency of documents and the size of classes (Persoon, 2026); firms and researchers read it as an external archive. In the setting studied here the upkeep is scheduled and contractual: the US office procures reclassification from contractors under a 10% maximum error rate, and a federal audit found four of them averaging 11.9%, 21.6%, 22.7% and 28.2% (US Department of Commerce, Office of Inspector General, 2023). Nothing in the arrangement ties the revision of one record to what happened to that record, although the areas chosen for revision may follow success (Arts and Veugelers, 2015, p. 1227). Outcome-blind maintenance is therefore the benchmark against which outcome dependence has to be shown.

passages.head: One record, several dated states, three readings
passages.text: Maintenance is continuous while the events a record describes are not, so one document accumulates several states of its own entry. A new US category was applied retroactively to granted patents meeting its criteria (Strumsky and Lobo, 2015); series rebuilt on the current scheme differ from historical data, and reclassified patents tend to be more cited (Lafond and Kim, 2019). The patent record is used here because its earlier states are published and dated rather than inferred.

passages.head: One record, several dated states, three readings
passages.text: The readings of section 2.1 make different predictions for a measure taken from such a record. Functional maintenance keeps entries fit for present search whatever happened to the case, so its updates should move a measure without tying it more closely to the outcome than the earlier record did. Decision-coupled writing completes entries when the organisation decides, so the density of a record follows the decision and the association with the outcome should be strongest in the state written at disposition. Reconstruction re-describes entries in the light of what later became of the case, so later revision should track later recognition.

passages.head: One record, several dated states, three readings
passages.text: Two cautions shape the design. Neither state of the record is a gold standard: reading past documents through the categories their authors had and through later ones are both legitimate (Bowker and Star, 1999, pp. 41-42). And a reversal across a binned exposure can arise from measurement error unrelated to the outcome (Dosemeci et al., 1990), so any movement has to be compared with what outcome-blind maintenance would produce.

passages.head: Four propositions
passages.text: The propositions were worded after the tests ran; their samples, thresholds and decision rules were frozen in advance, and Table S1 maps them onto the plan’s claims.

passages.head: Four propositions
passages.text: *P1. Vintage.* With documents, outcome and counting rule fixed, a novelty measure read from the current record is more positively associated with the outcome than the same measure read from the record as published. *Refuted by* a type-matched difference below 1 percentage point.

passages.head: Four propositions
passages.text: *P2a. Decision-coupled writing.* The record of a decided case is written again at its disposition, and the measure read at disposition is more strongly associated with the outcome than the record before it. The plan did not test this proposition; its evidence is descriptive.

passages.head: Four propositions
passages.text: *P2b. Outcome-dependent revision after the decision.* Classification information created after the decision is related to the decision. *Refuted by* an association inside a preregistered region of practical equivalence.

passages.head: Four propositions
passages.text: *P3. Reconstruction.* Revision made after an observation window closed tracks what the field later made of the invention. *Refuted by* no association with later recognition.

passages.head: Four propositions
passages.text: P1 is a measurement claim and needs no account of why the office writes what it writes. P2a and P2b separate a record written on the decision’s schedule from one rewritten after it. P3, the strongest, is examined in one channel only.

passages.head: Setting and record vintages
passages.text: The Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC), maintained jointly by the European Patent Office (EPO) and the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO), is a hierarchy of sections, classes, subclasses, main groups and subgroups, the level used here. A document carries inventive codes for what it claims and additional codes for further information; PatentsView labels the first kind inventional. Every symbol carries a validity date (EPO and USPTO, 2026), so the date a category came into existence is recorded rather than inferred, and the office publishes one document’s classification at more than one date.

passages.head: Setting and record vintages
passages.text: For the 896,097 first filings of Figure 2, filed 2013 to 2017 and disposed of by the data cut, the dated states arrive in a fixed order. An application is published a median 549 days after filing. The first examiner action follows at a median 689 days for later-granted applications and 726 for refused ones; allowance comes at a median 983 days and the grant at 1,106, while a refused application is abandoned at a median 1,185 days. The decision is the first notice of allowance or the terminal abandonment; disposition is the grant or the abandonment. Both records are maintained to the snapshot read here, early 2025.

passages.head: Setting and record vintages
passages.text: Three states follow. The record as published holds the classification printed at publication, before the decision, and nothing settled later. The grant-time record holds the classification reviewed when a granted application is passed to issue (USPTO, 2024, section 905.03(b)); a refused application has none. The current record holds every revision since, including symbols created after the decision. The record at disposition is the grant-time record for a granted application and, for a refused one, the record as published, the last state these files date before its abandonment.

passages.head: Setting and record vintages
passages.text: The population is 4,267,906 US applications filed between 2005 and 2018, published after filing, carrying at least one classification pair in PatentsView (USPTO, 2025) and matched to a prosecution history in the 2022 release of the Patent Examination Research Dataset (USPTO, 2023; Graham et al., 2018; Miller, 2020); 1,265,191 had no grant at the December 2024 data cut. Of 1,186,784 utility first filings carrying 2 to 25 scorable symbols of each type, 896,728 were filed 2015 to 2018; 875,870 of those were granted by the end of 2024 or terminally abandoned by June 2023, where the prosecution file ends; and 833,267 were published strictly before their own decision, the primary sample (Table S2). The office printed many more codes per publication from late 2014, and 59.3% of 2013 publications carrying an inventional symbol in the pair vocabulary have fewer than two, so the 2013 and 2014 cohorts are left out.

passages.head: Setting and record vintages
passages.text: The outcome is the grant. It is a decision that part of the recombination literature sets out to explain (Ferguson and Carnabuci, 2017), the prosecution history dates it to the day, and it is observed for applications that failed as well as those that succeeded, which a collection of granted patents cannot offer (Carley et al., 2015; Sampat and Williams, 2019).

passages.head: The measure
passages.text: The symbols on a document are read as the components an invention joins (Fleming, 2001) and taken in pairs (Verhoeven et al., 2016); the measure counts the pairs that appear on no earlier published document. Earlier is judged against a baseline of 48.5 million distinct pairs from 450 million pair instances on granted patents and pre-grant publications, classified as they are today. Both readings use this baseline, so the record as published means the focal codes as published, judged against prior art as now classified. Publication-time symbols retired before 2025 are dropped, and the two ways of keeping them are sensitivity checks (Table S3). Applications are compared in two bins, no new pair and five or more.

passages.head: What is held fixed and what is varied
passages.text: The design reads one maintained record at its own dates, as real-time analysis reads revised economic data by vintage (Croushore, 2011). The same applications, grant indicator, pairing rule, baseline and bins are used throughout section 5; only the state of each application’s record changes. The two conventional measures differ in two choices at once, which code types to count and which state to read, and in capping rules that this construction harmonises. All four combinations are estimated, and the contrast between the two conventional measures is split by the Shapley average of the two orderings (Shorrocks, 2013), with both orderings reported because the choices interact.

passages.head: Dating the information
passages.text: Two constructions make after the decision provable rather than asserted. An anachronistic code is a current code whose symbol’s validity date postdates the document’s publication: among pre-grant publications filed 2013 to 2018, excluding the Y cross-reference scheme, 14.42% of current code assignments are anachronistic and 37.66% of documents carry at least one. The post-horizon code is the stronger construction. The horizon is 1 January of the sixth year after filing, the dating tests use only applications disposed of before it, and a post-horizon symbol, valid from the horizon or later, could not have been on the record at the decision. Such a code is anchored when its main group, or a predecessor in a lineage map of 71,256 links over 17,107 symbols, is already in the record as published; it is a replacement when the current record has dropped a published symbol in the same area, and an addition otherwise. The proof is a lower bound: reassignment to symbols that already existed cannot be dated with these files.

passages.head: Estimation
passages.text: Every estimate is a linear probability model with absorbed fixed effects (Guimarães and Portugal, 2010), by default measure by filing year by technology field. Standard errors cluster on technology fields: the 34 WIPO fields recorded as an application’s first field, plus one cluster for applications without a field. Whether to cluster is a question about how units are sampled and assigned (Abadie et al., 2023), and field clusters are conservative here for both support and equivalence. Because the clusters are few, every deciding p-value is a restricted wild cluster bootstrap (Cameron et al., 2008) with Webb weights (Webb, 2023) and 9,999 draws, and intervals invert that test. Multiplicity is handled by Holm’s (1979) procedure within two families, and equivalence is judged on 90% intervals (Lakens et al., 2018). Nothing in the design identifies a causal effect.

passages.head: Pre-analysis plan
passages.text: Because analytic flexibility inflates false-positive rates (Simmons et al., 2011), the tests were set out in a pre-analysis plan for existing data (Weston et al., 2019), written after exploratory analysis of the same data had shown the sign reversal on a wider sample and the range of section 7, and frozen and hashed on 21 September 2026. The plan lists the results then known, which Table I marks, and only tests whose outcome was unknown at the freeze entered its verdict rule. It fixed each sample, outcome, model, predicted direction and smallest effect of interest (Lakens et al., 2018), and the rule mapping results onto a verdict (Table S1); for revision outcomes the smallest effect was the larger of .5 points and 10% of the outcome’s mean, set before any association with the grant or with citations was estimated. The timestamp rests on a local version-control commit and a SHA-256 lock file. The replication package (Anonymous, 2026) holds the lock file and the frozen files it hashes; the commit and five files that would identify the authors are withheld for anonymous review. After the freeze, four computational deviations and two code corrections were needed (Table S4); a rebuild reproduces every frozen estimate and moves no interval endpoint by more than one millionth. Analyses added after the freeze are labelled as such.

passages.head: Today and as published
passages.text: Figure 3(a) reads the same 833,267 applications at three dates. From today’s record, applications with five or more new pairs are 3.53 percentage points [+2.44, +4.67] more likely to be granted than those with none; from the record as published, the gap is -.60 [-1.44, +.29], not distinguishable from zero (p = .1711; Table S5). The design identifies the distance between the two readings rather than either level: +4.13 [+3.39, +4.95] on all code types and +3.68 [+3.06, +4.34] on inventional codes, both above the preregistered 2-point threshold (Holm-adjusted p = .0007) and on every sensitivity sample (Table S3).

passages.head: Vintage or the counting rule
passages.text: The two conventional measures, all code types read today and inventional codes read as published, differ by +4.27 [+3.33, +5.28]. The Shapley average assigns +3.90 [+3.24, +4.63] to the date of reading and +.37 [-.04, +.78] to the code type, p = .0801 (Figure 3(b)). The two orderings put the date’s share at 86% and 97%, because code type matters on today’s record (+.60 [+.14, +1.07]) and not on the record as published (+.14 [-.30, +.58]).

passages.head: The permutation benchmark
passages.text: A record that grew with no regard to outcomes would still move the association, because the later record is larger and grows unevenly across fields and cohorts. Permuting the grant within cells of filing year, technology field, code count and novelty bin as published moves the all-type difference by +.34 (+.33 for inventional codes), and the observed difference exceeds that by +3.79 (permutation p ≤ .0001). With finer cells, adding text novelty, applicant characteristics or the primary subclass as published, the excess stays between +3.46 and +3.83 (Table S6). The benchmark shows that today’s record carries information related to the grant that the record as published lacks. It cannot say whether that information was written because of the outcome, on the outcome’s schedule or because it describes the invention better; the reading at disposition separates the first two.

passages.head: Read at disposition
passages.text: Reading each application at disposition, from its grant-time record if granted and its record as published if refused, gives a gap of +16.77 [+14.91, +18.68] (Figure 3(a)). The rise from publication, +17.37 [+15.74, +19.11], is coupled to the decision by construction, since only a granted application receives the pass at issue. Later maintenance, which also reaches refused records, moves the gap back by -13.24 [-14.64, -11.84], so the difference of section 5.1 is the net of two large movements; inventional codes show the same pattern (+14.66 and -10.98; Table S6). Because a refused record may gain codes during pendency, which these files do not date, the reading at disposition is an upper bound. The vintage difference also falls by filing cohort, from +6.53 for 2015 to +2.05 for 2018, mainly because the rise at the grant shrinks (+20.32 to +13.77), partly offset by a smaller later fall (-13.79 to -11.72; Table S6).

passages.head: Breadth, cut and timing
passages.text: Part of what a count of new pairs records is breadth, since it rises with the number of symbols a record carries. With novelty measured as the share of an application’s pairs that are new, top decile against none, and the same fixed effects, today’s level is not distinguishable from zero for either code type, while the vintage difference is +2.04 [+1.24, +2.95] for all code types and +.69 [+.21, +1.20] for inventional codes (Table S6): the level read today is mostly breadth, and the difference survives, attenuated, for all-type symbols. Cutting each reading at the same ranks, top against bottom within-year quintile, gives +4.89 and +4.08, and among the 81.7% of applications published before their first examiner action the difference is +3.83 and +3.25. Documents also move between bins less than a published comparison implies: of applications in today’s top bin, 38.5% stay there as published and 21.9% fall to zero (Figure 3(c), Figure S1). In 30 of 31 subgroups the gap is lower as published, and its sign changes in 17 (Figure S2).

passages.head: Why the records diverge
passages.text: Table I lists the preregistered tests in the plan’s order, with what was known at the freeze and the label the frozen rule assigned, failures beside successes. Each estimate is an association between a feature of a record and an outcome recorded on it.

passages.head: What does not explain the difference
passages.text: The explanation raised for citations, and the one this paper set out to test for the grant, is that symbols introduced after a decision are applied backwards to the documents that turned out well (Fleming, 2001; Arts and Veugelers, 2015). The highest-priority test asked this of each record, using the validity dates. On 821,783 applications whose published main groups later received a post-horizon symbol, granted applications are more likely than refused ones to carry such a symbol, by +.40 points on a base of 13.87% (90% interval [+.155, +.652]), and to carry one that adds a new pair, by +.66 on 9.65% ([+.364, +.957]). Both intervals lie inside the preregistered bands of ±1.387 and ±.965, the second by eight thousandths of a point, which the frozen rule reads as a kill by equivalence (Table S7). The bands are 10% of each outcome’s base rate, not a share of the gap, and the test sees only new symbols. The association sits in additions (+.46 on a base of 2.92%), not in replacements of retired symbols (-.05, p = .7157). A direct counterfactual agrees in size: on the first filings of Figure 2, removing every code created after disposition moves the raw current-record gap from +6.16 to +5.46, and removing as many random codes, in one seeded draw, moves it to +5.56.

passages.head: What does not explain the difference
passages.text: A baseline of granted patents alone, as in Arts and Veugelers (2015), omits recombination that refused publications had disclosed, and the omission might be selective. On 3,202,512 first filings, removing never-granted publications from the baseline turns fewer pairs new than removing matched random sets of applications, by -.057 per first filing [-.078, -.037], against an equivalence threshold of .052 (Figure S3(c)). The sign is the opposite of the prediction: the baseline is a construction choice with consequences, not a bias of known sign.

passages.head: What does not explain the difference
passages.text: Scheme revision is not the carrier either. Applications whose published symbols no revision touched still show an excess of +4.11 over the benchmark, inside the +3.04 to +5.24 range of the exposed quintiles; the gradient runs in the predicted direction but is not monotone (Spearman +.90), and the top-minus-bottom difference of +2.20 (p = .0642) leaves that test inconclusive (Figure S4(b)).

passages.head: What does
passages.text: The largest movement is the second writing at the grant (section 5.4). On the 656,961 granted applications of Figure 2 with a grant-time record, mean new pairs run 2.85 at publication, 12.28 at the grant and 20.95 today, so 52.1% of the change is present at the grant itself, while a refused record, written once and then maintained, rises from 2.95 to 17.47. These timings are descriptive, not tests.

passages.head: What does
passages.text: A narrower channel looks reconstructive. Among 611,888 granted applications, granted from 2015, published by mid-2019 and matched to a single patent, carrying an anchored symbol introduced after the five-year forward-citation window closed rises by +1.55 points per standard deviation of log forward citations [+.88, +2.23], on a base of 9.06% (Holm-adjusted p = .0007). Its 90% interval, [+1.00, +2.11], lies above the smallest effect of interest, .906, and seven robustness variants run from +1.29 to +1.57 (Figure S4(a), Table S8). The plan’s verdict of partial support rests on this test. Because the symbol did not exist while the citations accrued, the citations cannot be its consequence. An exploratory test, however, finds a similar gradient among refused applications for symbols added after a three-year citation window (+.42 points per standard deviation of examiner citations and +.57 of applicant citations, standard errors .10 and .12), so revision follows attention to a document, as maintenance driven by use would also predict. Revision after the grant is unrelated to the patent’s stock-market value (Kogan et al., 2017): -.08 points per standard deviation on 180,196 granted applications, inside an equivalence threshold of 2.635 (p = .5849).

passages.head: What does
passages.text: Family records are maintained too. Continuations and divisions are +62.5 points more likely than first filings to record zero novelty, on 1,550,133 first filings and 428,713 such descendants, and removing the descendant’s own family documents from the prior art closes .977 [.959, .992] of that gap (Table S9, Figure S3(a)); continuations-in-part, which add new matter, show no premium. For families whose root was published from 2017, the premium is +25.9 [+22.8, +28.4] larger read today than as published, although that estimate fails its precision check. A premium is present at publication as well, 58.0% against 49.3%, so maintenance enlarges an inheritance rather than creating it.

passages.head: A measure the office cannot revise
passages.text: Text cannot be reclassified. Novelty measured as the share of a published abstract’s content bigrams that appear in no earlier abstract, adapted from Arts et al. (2021), is fixed at publication. Among the first filings of Figure 2 with a scorable abstract, the top text-novelty quintile within filing year is granted less often than the bottom one, by -8.18 points raw and -4.27 with filing year by field effects and the plan’s controls (cluster-robust standard error .82), on 358,438 applications. Its correlation with either code measure is near zero (.004 and .022), so the text measure records something else, and its agreement in sign with the record as published is an exploratory observation, not a validation.

passages.head: Inferential consequences
passages.text: Before the plan was written, the same question had been estimated under every defensible combination of six construction and modelling choices (Steegen et al., 2016): 432 specifications on 4,257,607 applications. Estimates run from -6.46 to +14.42 points, median -1.31 (Figure 4). Leaving out the 144 specifications restricted to software-exposed fields, which have three clusters, 132 intervals lie below zero, 126 span it and 30 lie above it, none of the last reading the record as published. The specification closest to published practice, today’s codes against a granted-patent baseline with every filing retained and no controls, returns +.31 [-2.15, +2.77]; the record as published with breadth controlled returns -4.09 [-5.08, -3.10]. As in a specification curve (Simonsohn et al., 2020), what matters is which choice carries the movement. Leverage, the largest median absolute change from swapping two levels of one choice, is 3.2 points for the novelty measure, 3.1 for whether related filings stay in, 3.1 for the control set, 1.9 for the novelty cut, 1.5 for the field restriction and 1.2 for the filing window (Figure 4(b)). The enumeration cannot separate the record’s state from the baseline or code type, which sit together in one choice; it locates the problem, and section 5 measures it.

passages.head: What the evidence says about codified memory
passages.text: The three readings of section 2.5 fare differently. Decision-coupled writing describes the largest movement: a granted record is written again at disposition and a refused one is not, which takes the association from -.60 to +16.77 points. Functional maintenance describes what happens next: datable information created after the decision is related to it only within the equivalence band, and maintenance that reaches refused records removes most of what the grant pass wrote. Reconstruction finds support in one channel, which cannot be told apart from maintenance driven by use.

passages.head: What the evidence says about codified memory
passages.text: For organisational memory, the result refines the storage view rather than replacing it. Entries are not rewritten in hindsight; they are written on the organisation’s own decision schedule, and when acquisition is coupled to decisions, the density of the record carries them. In the terms of section 2.3, the incentive to complete a record arrives with the decision, so codification effort is spent unevenly (Zollo and Winter, 2002) and on the outcome’s schedule. A secondary user who dates an entry by the event it describes, rather than by when it was written, inherits that coupling, and here it is large enough to change the conclusion a study would draw. Under partial support, the frozen plan allows only the claim that post-decision additions are related to the outcome, with the mechanism not identified; the account of decision-coupled writing rests on the descriptive reading at disposition added after the freeze and should be read with that status. The case answers the call to study how knowledge becomes embedded in memory over time (Casey and Olivera, 2011) with dated evidence, and it qualifies the functional view (Stein and Zwass, 1995): maintenance that reaches every entry dilutes the dependence that decision-coupled acquisition creates, and what remains is what a reader of today’s record inherits. Documentation completed on an outcome’s schedule is common, from incident reports written up on escalation to customer records enriched when a deal closes and case files completed at decision; this paper shows the consequence for one classification only.

passages.head: Implications for research
passages.text: Three asks follow, in ascending cost. Ask when the measure was written, not only what it says. If the artefact is versioned, read two versions and state which one an estimate comes from, since a second version is a join rather than a new data collection. If it is not versioned, ask whether entries are completed on the outcome’s schedule, because here coupling at the decision moves the estimate far more than datable revision after it. The most misleading reading mixes dates: a design that read granted cases from their records at disposition and refused ones from earlier records would find a gap near 17 points in these data. Two consequences are specific to recombination measures: a count of new pairs also counts how broadly a document has been classified, so breadth belongs in the model, and studies that build knowledge measures from patent classes should report the vintage they read.

passages.head: Implications for practice
passages.text: Knowledge managers who keep taxonomies, knowledge bases, customer or case records can apply the same logic. Store the date of each classification or tag assignment and keep superseded versions of the taxonomy, so that the repository can answer what it said on a given date. Before mining a repository for what predicts success, check whether entries are completed on the outcome’s schedule, for example reviews written only for completed projects or tags added when a deal closes, and compare a snapshot taken at the decision with the current one. Train analytic and predictive models on snapshots dated before the outcome, so that later entries cannot carry the outcome into the model, and let assistants that answer from a knowledge base log which version of each entry they read. For keepers of shared classifications such as the patent offices, dating each assignment and keeping superseded states as first-class objects would let historical users do directly what this paper could do only through symbol validity dates; differencing archived snapshots can bound assignment dates meanwhile. Accuracy is a separate question, and the federal audit reports initial contractor classifications above the contractual error maximum (US Department of Commerce, Office of Inspector General, 2023).

passages.head: Objections and scope
passages.text: The first objection is that today’s codes are simply better. They may be; the claim is only that the estimate moves with the state of the record, and the benchmark of section 5.3 cannot separate better description from outcome dependence, which is why the reading at disposition and the dating tests are needed. The second is that a change of sign across readings is what measurement error unrelated to the outcome can do to a binned exposure (Dosemeci et al., 1990); the reading at disposition locates the movement in the grant pass rather than in noise. The third, not ruled out, is that the classification as published is itself endogenous, because it shapes the search that decides the application; the paper compares two imperfect states and treats neither as clean. The fourth is that the clustering is thin, hence the bootstrap; the software-only specifications, on three clusters, decide nothing. The scope is one office, one scheme, one outcome and one family of count-based measures, on applications published from 2013.

passages.head: Conclusion, limitations and future research
passages.text: The classification studied here is maintained so that the next search succeeds. Read as a dated history, it returns an association between recombinant novelty and grant that is positive today, absent as published and large at disposition, depending on which of its own dates it is read from.

passages.head: Conclusion, limitations and future research
passages.text: Six things cannot be claimed. Nothing is causal: every estimate is an association, and the timing arguments establish only that information could not have been written before an event. Reassignment to existing symbols after the decision cannot be dated with these files and is not tested. The refused side of the reading at disposition is the record as published, so that reading is an upper bound. The plan was frozen after exploratory analysis of the same data, and the propositions were worded after the tests. Nothing is claimed for applications published before 2013. And neither state of the record is a truth against which the other can be scored.

passages.head: Conclusion, limitations and future research
passages.text: Future research can take the design to other versioned taxonomies, such as occupational, diagnostic and product classifications or skills ontologies, and to organisational repositories whose entries are completed on an outcome’s schedule. Differencing archived snapshots could date assignments to intervals, and records of refused applications recovered at abandonment would tighten the reading at disposition.

passages.head: Conclusion, limitations and future research
passages.text: A record kept for present retrieval is judged by whether the next search succeeds; a record used for historical inference has to be read back to a date. The scheme studied here is kept for the first purpose and used for the second.

passages.head: Data and code availability
passages.text: The replication package (Anonymous, 2026) holds the analysis scripts, the frozen plan, its lock file and the deviation log; the data are public (USPTO, 2023, 2025; EPO and USPTO, 2026; Kogan et al., 2025). The supplementary material holds Tables S1 to S9 and Figures S1 to S6, two of which show the companion web application that recomputes the headline quantities in the reader’s browser; its address is withheld for anonymous review.
